mediastore:1.text: One of the main components of Media Store is a server-side web front end, namely the Facade component, which delivers websites to the users and provides session management.

mediastore:3.text: To this end, the Facade component delivers the corresponding registration and log-in pages to users.

mediastore:6.text: In addition, users can browse, download, and upload audio files using the Facade component.

mediastore:7.text: Application business logic is provided by a central business logic component, called the MediaManagement component.

mediastore:8.text: The MediaManagement component coordinates the communication of other components.

mediastore:9.text: Furthermore, it fetches audio files from a specific location (e.g., a dedicated file server or a local disk) when processing download requests.

mediastore:11.text: The UserManagement component answers the requests for registration and authentication.

mediastore:12.text: The UserDBAdapter component queries the database.

mediastore:13.text: When a user logs into the system, Media Store does not store the password in plain text, but rather the UserManagement component implements further functions to hash and salt the passwords.

mediastore:16.text: The re-encoded files are then digitally and individually watermarked by the TagWatermarking component.

mediastore:17.text: Afterward, the MediaManagement component forwards these audio files from the TagWatermarking component to the user.

mediastore:19.text: To allow users to download several files at a time, we provide the Packaging component, which archives multiple audio files into a single compressed file.

mediastore:20.text: The ReEncoder component converts the bit rates of audio files.

mediastore:23.text: The Database component represents an actual database (e.g., MySQL).

mediastore:24.text: It stores user information and meta-data of audio files such as the name and the genre.

mediastore:25.text: After the user calls the page to list all available audio files, AudioAccess creates a query that is sent to the Database component.

mediastore:26.text: When a user uploads an audio file, the MediaAccess component stores it at the predefined location.

mediastore:27.text: The MediaAccess component encapsulates database access for meta-data of audio files.

mediastore:28.text: Furthermore, it fetches a list of all available audio files.

mediastore:29.text: By contrast, the UserDBAdapter component provides all functions required in order to encapsulate database access for the user data.

mediastore:30.text: The UserDBAdapter component creates a query based on the user's request.

mediastore:31.text: The Database component then executes the actual query for files.

mediastore:32.text: All salted hashes of passwords are also stored in the Database component.

mediastore:33.text: By contrast, all audio files are stored in a specific location (e.g., a dedicated file server or a local disk) to decouple the DataStorage from the database.

mediastore:34.text: When a user requests files to download, the MediaAccess component fetches the associated meta-data from the Database.

teastore:1.text: The TeaStore consists of 5 replicatable services and a single Registry instance.

teastore:2.text: The WebUI service retrieves images from the Image Provider.

teastore:3.text: Users are authenticated by the Auth service.

teastore:4.text: Data is retrieved from the PersistenceProvider and product recommendations from the Recommender service.

teastore:5.text: The WebUI provides the TeaStore front-end using Servlets in combination with JSP files.

teastore:6.text: It contains logic to save and retireve values from cookies.

teastore:7.text: Images (with few exceptions) are not provides by the WebUi, but are retrieved from the Image Provider service instead.

teastore:8.text: The UI provides a status page at link indicating the current state of the TeaStore.

teastore:10.text: The Image Provider delivers images to the WebUI as base64 encoded strings to embed them in the final HTML.

teastore:11.text: It matches the provided product ID or UI name (the filename for images not representing a product and therefore without product ID) and the image size to a unique image identifier.

teastore:12.text: If the product ID or UI name is not available to the Image Provider, a standard "not found" image will be delivered in the correct size.

teastore:18.text: The Auth service handles user and session authentication.

teastore:22.text: The Persistence service provides access to the data persisted in the relational database back-end.

teastore:23.text: It maps the relational entities to the JSON entity objects passed between services using the EclipseLink JPA ORM mapper.

teastore:24.text: It features endpoints for general CRUD-Operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) for the persistent entities.

teastore:25.text: The persistence provider uses a second level entity cache provided by the JPA implementation.

teastore:26.text: As such, it also acts as a caching layer.

teastore:27.text: The Recommender is used to generate individual product recommendations for each user.

teastore:28.text: It is trained using all existing orders.

teastore:37.text: The Registry provides information about how many service instances are online for each service and where they are located.

teastore:38.text: Service instances register themselves at the registry on startup.

teastore:41.text: Every running instance of the TeaStore uses one single registry.

teastore:43.text: By limiting it to a single registry instance, it enables easy configuration of multiple parallel TeaStores with minimal configuration overhead.

bigbluebutton:5.text: The HTML5 client is a single page, responsive web application that is built upon the following components, React.js for rendering the user interface in an efficient manner, WebRTC for sending/receiving audio and video.

bigbluebutton:6.text: The HTML5 client connects directly with the BigBlueButton server over port 443 (SSL), from loading the BigBlueButton client to making a web socket connection.

bigbluebutton:8.text: The HTML5 server sits behind nginx.

bigbluebutton:9.text: The HTML5 server is built upon Meteor.js in ECMA2015 for communication between client and server and upon MongoDB for keeping the state of each BigBlueButton client consistent with the BigBlueButton server.

bigbluebutton:10.text: The MongoDB database contains information about all meetings on the server and, in turn, each client connected to a meeting.

bigbluebutton:11.text: Each user's client is only aware of the their meeting's state, such the user's public and private chat messages sent and received.

bigbluebutton:12.text: The client side subscribes to the published collections on the server side.

bigbluebutton:13.text: Updates to MongoDB on the server side are automatically pushed to MiniMongo on the client side.

bigbluebutton:14.text: The following diagram gives an overview of the architecture of the HTML5 client and its communications with the other components in BigBlueButton.

bigbluebutton:19.text: BigBlueButton 2.3 moves away from a single nodejs process for bbb-html5 towards multiple nodejs processes handling incoming messages from clients.

bigbluebutton:20.text: This means that bbb-html5 could use multiple CPU cores for processing messages and handling browser sessions (each nodejs process runs on a single CPU core).

bigbluebutton:21.text: As of 2.3-alpha-7, bbb-html5 uses 2 "frontend" and two "backend" processes (this value is configurable in bbb-html5-with-roles.conf, see Configuration Files).

bigbluebutton:26.text: Frontends receive other DDP events including method calls to send events to akka-apps.

bigbluebutton:30.text: If more than one backend is running, bbb-web splits the load in round-robin fashion by assigning an instanceId.

bigbluebutton:37.text: BigBlueButton web application is a Java-based application written in Scala.

bigbluebutton:38.text: It implements the BigBlueButton API and holds a copy of the meeting state.

bigbluebutton:39.text: The BigBlueButton API provides a third-party integration (such as the BigBlueButtonBN plugin for Moodle) with an endpoint to control the BigBlueButton server.

bigbluebutton:47.text: Redis PubSub provides a communication channel between different applications running on the BigBlueButton server.

bigbluebutton:49.text: When a meeting is recorded, all events are stored in Redis DB.

bigbluebutton:52.text: BigBlueButton Apps is the main application that pulls together the different applications to provide real-time collaboration in the meeting.

bigbluebutton:53.text: It provides the list of users, chat, whiteboard, presentations in a meeting.

bigbluebutton:58.text: We have extracted out the component that integrates with FreeSWITCH into it’s own application.

bigbluebutton:60.text: Communication between apps and FreeSWITCH Event Socket Layer (fsels) uses messages through redis pubsub.

bigbluebutton:62.text: We think FreeSWITCH is an amazing piece of software for handling audio.

bigbluebutton:63.text: FreeSWITCH provides the voice conferencing capability in BigBlueButton.

bigbluebutton:65.text: Users joining through Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox are able to take advantage of higher quality audio by connecting using WebRTC.

bigbluebutton:66.text: FreeSWITCH can also be integrated with VOIP providers so that users who are not able to join using the headset will be able to call in using their phone.

bigbluebutton:70.text: The WebRTC-SFU acts as the media controller handling negotiations and to manage the media streams.

bigbluebutton:72.text: A user can join the voice conference (running in FreeSWITCH) from the BigBlueButton HTML5 client or through the phone.

bigbluebutton:73.text: When joining through the client, the user can choose to join Microphone or Listen Only, and the BigBlueButton client will make an audio connection to the server via WebRTC.

bigbluebutton:76.text: Uploaded presentations go through a conversion process in order to be displayed inside the client.

bigbluebutton:78.text: The PDF document is then converted into scalable vector graphics (SVG) via bbb-web.

bigbluebutton:79.text: The conversion process sends progress messages to the client through the Redis pubsub.

jabref:1.text: We have been successfully transitioning from a spaghetti to a more structured architecture with the model in the center, and the logic as an intermediate layer towards the gui which is the outer shell.

jabref:2.text: There are additional utility packages for preferences and the cli.

jabref:4.text: We have JUnit tests to detect violations of the most crucial dependencies (between logic, model, and gui), and the build will fail automatically in these cases.

jabref:5.text: The model represents the most important data structures (BibDatases, BibEntries, Events, and related aspects) and has only a little bit of logic attached.

jabref:6.text: The logic is responsible for reading/writing/importing/exporting and manipulating the model, and it is structured often as an API the gui can call and use.

jabref:7.text: Only the gui knows the user and his preferences and can interact with him to help him solve tasks.

jabref:9.text: The model should have no dependencies to other classes of JabRef and the logic should only depend on model classes.

jabref:10.text: The cli package bundles classes that are responsible for JabRef’s command line interface.

jabref:11.text: The preferences represents all information customizable by a user for her personal needs.

jabref:12.text: We use an event bus to publish events from the model to the other layers.
